channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Research highlights long-term health risks of gestational diabetes
item.description: Gestational diabetes is often viewed as a complication of pregnancy that resolves after delivery, but a new review led by researchers from LSU's Pennington Biomedical Research Center shows that its health implications can extend for years, increasing cardiometabolic risks for mothers and potentially affecting the future health of their children.

item.title: ICE operation in Minneapolis likely led to fewer health care visits for Spanish-speaking patients, analysis finds
item.description: From December 2025 through February 2026, about 2,000 US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents descended on the Minneapolis-Saint Paul metro area, which increased raids, arrests, and violence as part of Operation Metro Surge (OMS).

item.title: Eye trauma from high-velocity pickleball may heighten glaucoma risk, doctors warn
item.description: Being hit in the eye by a high-velocity pickleball may heighten the risk of glaucoma, doctors warn in the online journal BMJ Case Reports after treating a female player with this injury.

item.title: Childhood diet high in fruit and fish linked to lower Crohn's disease risk
item.description: A high intake of salty snacks during the teenage years is linked to a heightened risk of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)—Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis or a mix of both—in young adulthood, finds a large long-term study published online in the journal Gut.

item.title: Music before and during coronary angiography linked to lower blood pressure
item.description: Music therapy before and during an often stressful procedure to visualize blood flow to coronary arteries (coronary angiography) is associated with lower systolic blood pressure—the higher number in a reading—according to the results of a comparative clinical trial published online in the journal Heart.

item.title: From primal instinct to persistent preoccupation: Measuring 'food noise'
item.description: How people think about food continues to evolve. For early hunter-gatherers, food meant survival. Thoughts about food focused mainly on where to find it. As people learned to farm, thoughts about food shifted from something hunted or caught to something cultivated.

item.title: Parents strongly accept intestinal ultrasound for pediatric IBD monitoring
item.description: Parents of children with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) report strong acceptance of intestinal ultrasound (IUS) for disease monitoring, according to a study published online Nov. 17 in JPGN Reports.

item.title: Could blowing your nose make cold symptoms worse?
item.description: Few things are more frustrating than dealing with a runny nose when you're sick. No matter how many times you blow your nose, a few minutes later it's full of snot again and the sniffles are back.

item.title: Many languages, one common neural code
'I'm amazed every day': Woman marks one year with a pig kidney
item.description: A New Hampshire woman has now lived for one year with a kidney from a gene-edited pig, the longest any patient is known to have done so.

item.title: Significant decrease in Black-white mortality gap during past 30 years
item.description: A major health gap in America is shrinking. A new study by researchers at the American Cancer Society (ACS) shows the historic divide in death rates between Black and white men and women in the United States narrowed dramatically between 1993 and 2023. Excess mortality among Black adults plummeted by 56% for men and 68% for women.

item.title: AI can predict antidepressant response, but does not understand all patients equally
item.description: George Mason University researchers have revealed just how much health literacy can influence AI's ability to understand patients. In a new study involving simulated patients, an AI antidepressant decision aid correctly identified medical information 82% of the time when patients used precise medical language, but less than half the time when they described their health in vaguer or more informal terms.

item.title: When antidepressants don't help, could ketamine be an option?
item.description: Once known mainly as a surgical anesthetic, ketamine is now an option for people whose depression hasn't eased with standard medications and therapy.

item.title: How the brain's visual system shapes lasting fear memories
item.description: Researchers at McGovern Medical School at UTHealth Houston have discovered how the brain's visual system plays an active role in transforming threatening experiences into lasting fear memories and how noninvasive brain stimulation can interrupt this process.

item.title: Not just a phase: Measuring the long-term toll of high school substance use
item.description: High schoolers who smoke cigarettes, use cannabis or take other drugs face a higher risk of dying earlier in adulthood, according to a five-decade University of Michigan study.

item.title: New Year's resolutions: Starting small today could work better than waiting until January
item.description: Every year, millions of people promise to start the new year by losing weight, eating better and exercising more. January feels like a natural moment for a fresh start. But big resolutions create a lot of pressure and are hard to keep up.

item.title: Lack of data hinders genetic screening for heart failure in the Brazilian population
item.description: The low representation of Brazilians in global genomic databases compromises the accuracy of tests used to investigate the causes of heart failure. This is according to a study by the University of São Paulo (USP), which revealed an additional limitation of these tests: interpreting results is significantly more difficult when analyzing DNA segments of African or Indigenous ancestry.

item.title: How sensory neurons help the brain pursue its goals
item.description: A new Yale study offers insight into a fundamental question in neuroscience: How does the nervous system transform sensory information into signals that help us achieve our goals?

item.title: For your health—shedding light on family history and cancer risk
item.description: If you ask some of your friends to name three things that increase the risk of cancer, it'd be likely that some version of "family history" would make most of their lists.

item.title: One in 12 children with Lyme disease show signs of Powassan virus co-infection
item.description: The prevalence of Powassan virus infection in U.S. children with suspected Lyme disease is higher than previously thought, according to a new study published in Clinical Infectious Diseases.

item.title: Only 13% of lung cancer patients would qualify for advance screening based on eligibility guidelines
item.description: A new data analysis of Southern California lung cancer patients has found that only 13% would have met eligibility criteria for advance screening despite expanded eligibility guidelines issued in 2021. Female, Asian and Hispanic patients were significantly less likely to be eligible for lung cancer screening. The findings from the new study in the Journal of the American College of Radiology highlight the limited reach of existing eligibility criteria, especially in underrepresented populations.

item.title: Cholesterol plaques in the neck and legs signal increased cardiac risk
item.description: Atherosclerosis does not respect anatomical territories. Once cholesterol plaques appear in the arteries, they tend to spread throughout different regions of the arterial system. A new analysis from the PESA (Progression of Early Subclinical Atherosclerosis) study, led by researchers at the Centro Nacional de Investigaciones Cardiovasculares Carlos III (CNIC) under the direction of principal investigator Dr. Valentín Fuster, shows that the presence and extent of plaques in the neck (carotid) and leg (femoral) arteries are closely associated with the presence, severity and burden of atherosclerosis in the coronary arteries.

item.title: Whole-genome sequencing study reveals how antibiotic-resistant bacteria may spread through rural communities in Malawi
item.description: A new study led by researchers at Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine (LSTM) has shed light on how antibiotic-resistant bacteria spread within rural communities in Malawi.

item.title: T cells gone viral: New study finds host genetics shape the brain's immune response to chronic herpesvirus infection
item.description: Scientists have long suspected a common human herpesvirus contributed to the development of multiple sclerosis, a disease affecting the central nervous system and a leading cause of disability in young adults. A new study published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) demonstrates genetically determined differences in host control of a similar herpesvirus in mice are a major risk factor for allowing T cells to enter the brain and may offer clues to why only a fraction of the population infected with Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) develops MS.

item.title: Older drivers are not making the roads unsafe, research shows
item.description: Changes to medical fitness testing for South Australian drivers have not made the roads less safe, a new report from Adelaide University has found.

item.title: Can AI expedite medical imaging? Yes—if we can trust the picture
item.description: When it comes to medical imaging, everyone wants better technology faster—but no one wants to cut corners on health and safety. Enter a new statistical tool that determines whether AI-generated data could accurately stand in for patient data in clinical trials.

item.title: Fatigue can persist even after a good recovery from stroke
item.description: In a study of life after stroke, one survivor described doing less during the day if they planned to see friends that evening. When you're living with fatigue, even an ordinary day can take that kind of planning. Going out may mean deciding what else can wait until tomorrow.

item.title: Inflammatory sensor offers a target for new therapies in patients with brain injuries
item.description: A traumatic brain injury can have a lasting impact on a person's life. Beyond the immediate damage caused by the impact, subsequent processes can further impair brain function. These include inflammatory responses, which normally support defense and repair but can contribute to additional damage when strongly or persistently activated.

item.title: One in four students turn to AI for mental health support
item.description: New research finds students are using AI for emotional support, including when distressed and as a personal therapist or coach.

item.title: Everyday commute keeps drivers' hearts 'on duty,' study shows
item.description: The inactive routine of a driver's morning commute is associated with sustained cardiac activation, potentially carrying long-term health implications, according to new research from the University of Houston.
